extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics educators (researchers, teachers, and advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the quality and lasting importance of mathematical work and for effective mathematical exposition and teaching, emphasizing conceptual clarity, simplification, and pedagogy rather than technical accumulation. Drawn from André Weil's 1950 essay 'The Future of Mathematics.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification as the core criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The great mathematical ideas are simplifying ideas; the creator must be one who clarifies the most complicated tissues of formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical contribution is valuable when it reduces complexity and clarifies; works that merely multiply technical machinery without corresponding clarification are suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiplying technical machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematician's job is not to multiply technical machinery but to clarify; additions of complexity must be compensated by genuine clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work increases formal apparatus without producing simplification or insight, it should be treated critically. Prefer approaches that remove unnecessary machinery or show why it is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational reach over painstaking detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics 'is not a science that prospers on details painstakingly collected.' Significance and foundational reach matter more than mere accumulation of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a result or piece of work addresses important, wide-reaching problems or whether it is primarily an exercise in collecting technical particulars with limited conceptual payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing conceptual unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that reveal an underlying unity across apparently disparate areas are valued more than incremental refinements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is due to expositions or results that show relations between areas or compress disparate facts under a single principle; incremental or narrowly technical advances score lower on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival under future simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge current apparatus by whether future mathematicians will see it as essential or merely transient — whether key ideas will 'survive' future reorganizations and simplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical examples (e.g., Apollonius's conic-section detail becoming inessential) as a warning that techniques tied tightly to present notation or methods may not endure. Prefer ideas likely to remain after later simplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding over memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowledge of a proof means the understanding of its machinery and the ability to reconstruct it.' A reader who can recite but not reconstruct does not understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition should enable reconstruction: proofs and arguments must be presented so that a competent reader can rederive them, not merely verify line-by-line. Teaching should test reconstruction, not rote recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to the most general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching and exposition should follow 'the method which is related to the most general principles' rather than chasing local elegance or speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods and presentations tied to general principles; avoid strategies that prioritize clever shortcuts or isolated tricks at the expense of conveying broader conceptual frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear logical distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The student/reader must distinguish premises and conclusion, necessary and sufficient conditions, and a theorem from its converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition explicitly states hypotheses and conclusions, highlights what is necessary versus what is merely sufficient, and calls attention to converses or non-equivalences to prevent confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual excitement and exposure to the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Good exposition brings the reader 'to the brink of the unknown' — exposing live questions and open problems, not only settled answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-quality exposition stimulates curiosity by indicating where understanding stops and what questions remain; it does not present mathematics as a closed body of facts only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not merely accumulate facts; reveal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should reveal principles rather than merely accumulate facts or results disconnectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a paper or lecture, ask whether it organizes facts around explanatory principles; if it only collects results without showing why they belong together, its value is limited.
